guide.title: Campitelli, Rome: the Capitoline, the Roman Forum and the Palatine
guide.intro: Campitelli is the tenth of Rome's twenty-two rioni, and it is two very different places sharing one boundary. Most of its area is archaeology: the Roman Forum, run by the Parco archeologico del Colosseo, the Palatine hill above it, and the southern half of the Imperial Fora strip. Over the Forum stands the Capitoline, where the Musei Capitolini occupy the palaces around a square their own site credits to Michelangelo, and on its northern slope the Vittoriano. The rest is a small inhabited quarter of a few squares, some Mannerist and Baroque palaces, a working theatre and a short list of places to eat. Nearly every edge of the rione is a street or a square that is itself the boundary, so several things visitors assume are in Campitelli, including the Theatre of Marcellus, are not.

sections.heading: The shape of the rione
sections.body: Campitelli's edges are, almost everywhere, streets and squares that are themselves the boundary, which is why so much that visitors file under "Campitelli" turns out to sit next door. it.wikipedia's article on the rione lists them: via e piazza San Marco with Pigna, piazza Madonna di Loreto with Trevi, via dei Fori Imperiali with Monti, via di San Gregorio with Celio, then via dei Cerchi, piazza Sant'Anastasia, via di San Teodoro, via dei Fienili, piazza della Consolazione, vico Jugario and via di Monte Caprino with Ripa, and via Montanara, piazza di Campitelli, via Cavalletti, via dei Delfini, piazza e vicolo Margana and via dell'Aracoeli with Sant'Angelo. Three consequences are worth knowing before you walk it. The church of Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli is not in Campitelli: it.wikipedia's article on it opens by placing it in the rione Sant'Angelo. OpenStreetMap's boundary data and Nominatim both put the Theatre of Marcellus in Sant'Angelo as well, although businesses addressed on via del Teatro di Marcello are inside Campitelli, since a street name is not a claim on the monument it is named for. And piazza Venezia is genuinely unsettled: four sources give three different rioni for it, so this guide states no rione for the square at all and lets the Vittoriano, which comes back Campitelli on every method tested, carry the geography. The northern edge matters most. Via dei Fori Imperiali is the boundary with Monti, and the archaeological strip on either side of it is split down the middle: the Foro di Cesare, the Foro di Nerva with its temple of Minerva, the Tempio della Pace and Via Alessandrina are on the Campitelli side, while Trajan's Forum, Trajan's Column, Trajan's Markets and the Forum of Augustus are on the Monti side. Almost every guidebook treats the Imperial Fora as one thing in Monti. They are not.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body: The Capitoline is reached on foot from below. it.wikipedia describes the Cordonata as running from via del Teatro di Marcello up to the piazza del Campidoglio, designed by Michelangelo for Paul III in 1534-38 and partly modified by Giacomo Della Porta; it also says the basilica of Santa Maria in Aracoeli is reached by the Scalinata dell'Ara Coeli, which climbs alongside. OpenStreetMap maps three more named ways on the hill: the Rampa Caffarelli, the Scala dell'Arce Capitolina and the ancient Clivus Capitolinus. The Musei Capitolini give Piazza del Campidoglio 1, 00186 Roma as the address of the Capitoline complex. For the archaeological side, the Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes a walkway through the Imperial Fora entering at the Trajan's Column end and leaving at the Foro di Cesare on via Bonella, passing beneath via dei Fori Imperiali. The entrance stands in the rione Monti and the exit in Campitelli; the road between them is the boundary.

sections.heading: Tickets, hours and the World Heritage record
sections.body: Two ticketing systems cover most of what people come to Campitelli for, and different bodies run them. The Musei Capitolini are municipal, and their own site gives daily opening 09.30-19.30 with last admission an hour before closing, 09.30-14.00 on 24 and 31 December, 11.00-20.00 on 1 January 2026, and closure on 1 May and 25 December; from February 2026 that site states that admission is free for residents of Roma and the Citta Metropolitana on production of an identity card. The Roman Forum is run by the Parco archeologico del Colosseo. Its hours and the EUR 18,00 Forum Pass Super are given here as the Sovrintendenza Capitolina publishes them, not as the Parco gives them. Named tickets have been required for all admissions to the Parco archeologico del Colosseo since 18 October 2023. Check with the Parco before travelling. UNESCO records the World Heritage property Historic Centre of Rome, the Properties of the Holy See in that City Enjoying Extraterritorial Rights and San Paolo Fuori le Mura (ref. 91) as first inscribed in 1980, with a significant boundary modification in 1990 that extended the property to the walls of Urban VIII, the Holy See's extraterritorial properties and San Paolo fuori le Mura, and minor modifications in 2015 and 2023; the criteria are (i)(ii)(iii)(iv)(vi), the property 1,469.7 ha and the buffer zone 7,158.933 ha. UNESCO's brief synthesis describes the property as encompassing the whole historic centre of Rome within the city walls at their widest extent in the 17th century. UNESCO's record names no rione.

faq.question: What is actually in Campitelli?
faq.answer: Two ticketed archaeological enclosures - the Roman Forum and the Palatine - plus the southern half of the Imperial Fora, the Capitoline hill with the piazza del Campidoglio and the Musei Capitolini, and the Vittoriano on the hill's northern slope. Outside those, the inhabited part of the rione is small: piazza d'Aracoeli, a handful of Mannerist and Baroque palaces, about a dozen churches, a working theatre and six or seven places to eat.

faq.question: How much are the Capitoline Museums, and when are they open?
faq.answer: The museum's own site gives daily opening 09.30-19.30, last admission an hour before closing, 09.30-14.00 on 24 and 31 December, 11.00-20.00 on 1 January 2026, and closure on 1 May and 25 December. From February 2026 the site states that admission is free for residents of Roma and the Citta Metropolitana on production of an identity card. For non-residents the site gives, in the absence of temporary exhibitions, EUR 15,00 full and EUR 9,50 reduced; with the exhibitions running when this page was checked on 2 September 2026, EUR 20,50 full and EUR 15,00 reduced, a ticket which the site states does not admit to exhibitions at Villa Caffarelli. Online, 060608 and box-office presale carry a EUR 1,00 booking fee, and presold tickets are stated to be non-refundable and non-changeable. Tariffs change with the exhibition programme; check the museum's own page.

faq.question: What does it cost to get into the Roman Forum and the Palatine?
faq.answer: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the Forum Pass Super as EUR 18,00 full, valid for the day across the Foro Romano, the Fori Imperiali and the Palatino. That is a third party republishing the operator's tariff, not the Parco archeologico del Colosseo itself, so check with the Parco before travelling. Named tickets have been required for all admissions to the Parco since 18 October 2023.

faq.question: Can you go up the Vittoriano?
faq.answer: VIVE, the Ministry of Culture institute that runs the complex, describes a panoramic terrace, also called the terrazza delle Quadrighe, standing at seventy metres with a 360-degree view and reached by lifts, with two bronze quadrigas at the lift exit standing for the Unity and the Liberty of Italy. it.wikipedia's infobox gives the monument's overall height as 81 metres and its roof height as 70. The Ala Fori Imperiali, the wing facing via dei Fori Imperiali, is a separate space and VIVE's page describes it as under complete restoration and due to open.

faq.question: Which churches in Campitelli publish opening times?
faq.answer: Very few. San Sebastiano al Palatino is run by the Fraternite Monastique de Jerusalem, whose own site publishes the week's prayer times. Santa Maria Annunziata a Tor de' Specchi is recorded by it.wikipedia as open to the public only on 9 March, the feast of Santa Francesca Romana. The Nobile Collegio Chimico Farmaceutico, in and above San Lorenzo in Miranda, publishes no opening hours on its own site - only guided visits by booking. For Santa Maria in Aracoeli, Santa Francesca Romana, San Teodoro al Palatino, San Bonaventura al Palatino, Santi Cosma e Damiano and the Carcere Mamertino, no reachable official source gave hours, so this guide publishes none.

faq.question: Is the Imperial Fora walk in Campitelli or in Monti?
faq.answer: Both, and the split is the point. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina describes a walkway entering at the Trajan's Column end and leaving at the Foro di Cesare on via Bonella, passing beneath via dei Fori Imperiali. The entrance stands in Monti and the exit in Campitelli; the road between them is the boundary between the two rioni.

photos.title: Piazza del Campidoglio
photos.description: The Palazzo dei Conservatori across the piazza del Campidoglio on the Capitoline, with the square's star paving and the equestrian Marcus Aurelius on its plinth.
photos.author: Serghei Topor from Chisinau, Moldova

places.name: Piazza del Campidoglio
places.summary: The square on top of the Capitoline, with the Palazzo Senatorio at its head and a museum palace on either side. The Musei Capitolini's own site says the piazza in its present form was designed around the middle of the sixteenth century by Michelangelo Buonarroti, and that the palaces, the sculpture and the paving were carried out over the following centuries with additions and changes.
places.history: The same site's account of the ancient hill describes two summits, the Capitolium and the Arx, separated by a valley corresponding to today's square, whose level was about eight metres below the present one. Besides the square itself, OpenStreetMap maps four named ways and stairs on the hill: the Rampa Caffarelli, the Scala dell'Arce Capitolina, the Scalinata dell'Ara Coeli and the Clivus Capitolinus.

places.name: Palazzo Senatorio
places.summary: Palazzo Senatorio stands at Piazza del Campidoglio 1, the address the Musei Capitolini give for the Capitoline complex; it houses the Comune di Roma. it.wikipedia dates the building to the first half of the 12th century, on the ruins of the Tabularium, with a 16th-century refacing under Michelangelo and Giacomo Della Porta.

places.name: Musei Capitolini
places.summary: The Comune's museums on the Capitoline, occupying the Palazzo dei Conservatori, the Palazzo Nuovo and the Palazzo Caffarelli around the piazza del Campidoglio. The museum's own site gives daily opening 09.30-19.30, with last admission one hour before closing, 09.30-14.00 on 24 and 31 December, 11.00-20.00 on 1 January 2026, and closure on 1 May and 25 December; the contact line is the 060608 call centre, daily 09.00-19.00. From February 2026 the museum's own site states that admission is free for residents of Roma and the Citta Metropolitana on production of an identity card. For non-residents the site gives, in the absence of temporary exhibitions, EUR 15,00 full and EUR 9,50 reduced; with the exhibitions running when this page was checked on 2 September 2026, EUR 20,50 full and EUR 15,00 reduced, a ticket which the site states does not admit to exhibitions at Villa Caffarelli. Online, 060608 and box-office presale carry a EUR 1,00 booking fee, and presold tickets are stated to be non-refundable and non-changeable. Tariffs change with the exhibition programme; check the museum's own page.
places.history: The museum's own history page dates the birth of the Musei Capitolini to 1471, when Pope Sixtus IV gave the Roman people a group of bronze statues. Its page on the piazza and the palaces names the Protomoteca Capitolina among the museum's rooms. The Lupa Capitolina, a bronze she-wolf, is held in the Musei Capitolini.

places.name: Palazzo dei Conservatori
places.summary: One of the two palaces flanking the piazza del Campidoglio, and part of the Musei Capitolini. it.wikipedia gives its architects as Michelangelo Buonarroti and Giacomo Della Porta, says it was commissioned by the Comune di Roma, and explains the name: the elective city magistracy of the Conservatori sat there for four centuries.

places.name: Palazzo Nuovo
places.summary: The museum palace facing the Palazzo dei Conservatori across the piazza del Campidoglio. it.wikipedia says it was built in the seventeenth century under Girolamo and then Carlo Rainaldi and completed in 1663, and that the facade design is attributed to Michelangelo.
places.history: The colossal statue known as Marforio stands in its courtyard.

places.name: Palazzo Caffarelli al Campidoglio
places.summary: A museum wing on the Capitoline, also called Palazzo Clementino Caffarelli or Villa Caffarelli. it.wikipedia describes it as a sixteenth-century Caffarelli residence, later the Prussian embassy, expropriated by the Italian state after the First World War, then partly demolished and rebuilt as a municipal museum linked to the Musei Capitolini; it names Gregorio Canonica as the architect.

places.name: Cordonata Capitolina
places.summary: The wide ramped stair from via del Teatro di Marcello up to the piazza del Campidoglio. it.wikipedia says it was designed in 1534-38 by Michelangelo for Paul III and partly modified by Giacomo Della Porta, that the Dioscuri groups were placed on the balustrade in 1583 and the Trofei di Mario in 1590, and that black basalt lion fountains stand at the foot.

places.name: Fontana della Dea Roma
places.summary: The fountain set into the front of the Palazzo Senatorio. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the author as Matteo Bartolani da Citta di Castello, dates it 1588-1589, describes it in marble, and records that it was originally fed by the Acqua Felice.
places.history: The same Sovrintendenza page records that the Nile and Tiger colossi, the second later read as the Tiber, were placed by Michelangelo on plinths in 1543; that the central niche took a Minerva in 1583; and that in 1593 that figure was replaced by a small seated Domitianic Minerva in porphyry and marble.

places.name: Marforio
places.summary: A Roman colossal statue in the courtyard of the Palazzo Nuovo, inside the Musei Capitolini, and one of Rome's talking statues. it.wikipedia describes it as first-century marble, possibly Neptune, Oceanus or the Tiber, found around 1510 in the Forum of Augustus.

places.name: Tabularium
places.summary: The Roman public-record building beneath the Palazzo Senatorio, with an arcaded facade onto the Forum. it.wikipedia describes it as now forming part of the Musei Capitolini circuit.

places.name: Rupe Tarpea
places.summary: The Tarpeian Rock, the cliff on the south side of the Capitoline, as described by it.wikipedia. The church of Santa Maria della Consolazione stands at its foot.

places.name: Belvedere Tarpeo (Giardino di Monte Caprino)
places.summary: A public garden and viewpoint on the Capitoline, mapped in OpenStreetMap as a park under the name Belvedere Tarpeo at 41.891482, 12.4818829. That is the whole of what a reachable source establishes about it.

places.name: Terrazza Caffarelli
places.summary: Terrazza Caffarelli, an events venue at Piazzale Caffarelli 4.

places.name: Vittoriano (Monumento Nazionale a Vittorio Emanuele II)
places.summary: VIVE, the Ministry of Culture institute that runs the complex, states that it was conceived in January 1878, in the days after the death of Italy's first king, and inaugurated in 1911; VIVE's history gives Giuseppe Sacconi as its architect, building from 1885 to 1905. it.wikipedia's infobox gives the inauguration as 4 June 1911, a construction period of 1885-1935, and a height of 81 metres.
places.history: VIVE's own history of the monument runs from a decision of the Italian government after the king's death in 1878, through Vittorio Emanuele III's pressure on the site so that it could open in 1911, the fiftieth anniversary of unification, and the burial of the Unknown Soldier that turned it into a shrine. VIVE records that in the last years of the Second World War its basements sheltered Roman civilians, that after the war it was closed to the public and tried for "offesa estetica", and that it was relaunched under President Ciampi. It stands on piazza Venezia; no source states which rione that square belongs to, so none is stated for it.

places.name: Altare della Patria and the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier
places.summary: VIVE describes the Altare della Patria as conceived by Giuseppe Sacconi as an integral part of the design of the Vittoriano, with a sculpted frieze by Angelo Zanelli. VIVE states that it received the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in 1921, to commemorate the dead of the First World War, and that a laurel wreath is still laid there at official ceremonies. The tomb has a guard of honour.
places.history: VIVE notes that very many people use the name Altare della Patria for the whole of the Vittoriano, which is worth knowing when you are reading signs or asking directions.

places.name: Terrazza Panoramica del Vittoriano
places.summary: VIVE describes the panoramic terrace, also called the terrazza delle Quadrighe, as standing at seventy metres with a 360-degree view, reached by lifts; two bronze quadrigas at the lift exit stand for the Unity and the Liberty of Italy. it.wikipedia's infobox gives the monument's overall height as 81 metres and its roof height as 70.

places.name: Museo Centrale del Risorgimento al Vittoriano
places.address: Via di San Pietro in Carcere, Roma RM
places.summary: VIVE states the museum was conceived in 1884 but opened only in 1970. it.wikipedia gives the exhibition spaces as created in 1935 and opened in 1970, at via di San Pietro in Carcere on the left flank of the Vittoriano, administered by the Istituto per la storia del Risorgimento italiano.
places.history: The Istituto per la storia del Risorgimento italiano's own site is live and names the museum. VIVE gives the museum's coverage as the eighteenth century to the First World War.

places.name: Ala Fori Imperiali (ex Ala Brasini)
places.summary: VIVE describes the Ala Fori Imperiali, designed by Armando Brasini between the 1920s and 1930s with its own entrance onto via dei Fori Imperiali, as under complete restoration and due to open (VIVE's page, checked 2 September 2026).
places.history: VIVE records that the wing was originally intended to house the Museo Centrale del Risorgimento.

places.name: Sepolcro di Gaio Publicio Bibulo
places.summary: A Roman tomb of the early first century BC, at the foot of the Vittoriano on via del Teatro di Marcello.
places.history: it.wikipedia describes it as built of tufo dell'Aniene and travertine, with a surviving height of 4.76 m; only the west wall and a fragment of the south-west corner of the cella remain, and the podium is largely buried because the ancient street level was far lower than today's.

places.name: Insula dell'Ara Coeli
places.summary: A second-century Roman apartment block at the foot of the Capitoline, in the angle between the Ara Coeli staircase and the Vittoriano. it.wikipedia describes it as brick, resting on an opus-reticulatum wall probably of the first century built to consolidate the hill.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that in the Middle Ages the upper part of the insula was occupied by the church of San Biagio de Mercato, later replaced by Santa Rita da Cascia, and that the block above was dismantled in the 1930s for the Vittoriano works, which is when the insula itself was found. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's page on Santa Rita independently confirms that the medieval San Biagio "de mercato" stood on that site.

places.name: Monumento a Cola di Rienzo
places.summary: A statue in the planted area on the left flank of the Cordonata. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the statue to Girolamo Masini (1840-1885) and the base to Francesco Azzurri (1827-1901), and dates the work "1871 realizzazione statua; 1886-1887 realizzazione monumento", in bronze, marble and brick facing.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza records that the city council authorised the purchase in 1886, that the base reuses ancient marble reliefs partly taken from the Ara Coeli staircase, that the monument was unveiled without ceremony on 20 September 1887, and that it carries no dedicatory inscription beyond "Cola de Rienzi" cut into the bronze.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Aracoeli
places.summary: A minor basilica on the Arx, the northern summit of the Capitoline, which it.wikipedia says is reached by the Scalinata dell'Ara Coeli. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the church was originally called Santa Maria in Capitolio and formed part of the monastery complex on the hill, that the present name is attested from 1323, and that construction runs from the thirteenth to the eighteenth century, Gothic and then Baroque.

places.name: Basilica di Santa Francesca Romana (Santa Maria Nova)
places.address: Piazza di Santa Francesca Romana 4, Roma RM
places.summary: A basilica at piazza di Santa Francesca Romana 4. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia says the church was built about the middle of the ninth century on an earlier oratory under Paul I, and that after a tenth-century restoration it was rededicated as Santa Maria Nova to distinguish it from Santa Maria Antiqua in the Forum. The Antiquarium Forense occupies rooms of its former monastery.

places.name: Basilica dei Santi Cosma e Damiano
places.summary: A minor basilica on via dei Fori Imperiali, built into the Tempio della Pace. it.wikipedia dates it to the sixth century and calls it the mother house of the Franciscan Third Order Regular since 1512. No source states its hours or Mass times, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia describes the church as built into the Tempio della Pace, occupying part of that imperial forum's fabric. That forum lies on the south side of via dei Fori Imperiali, the boundary with Monti.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Luca e Martina
places.summary: A church on the Capitoline slope. it.wikipedia says it was begun in 1634 and finished in 1664.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the church was originally dedicated to Santa Martina and founded in the seventh century, probably by Honorius I, and that it is a rectory within the parish of San Marco Evangelista al Campidoglio.

places.name: Chiesa di San Giuseppe dei Falegnami
places.summary: The carpenters' church, standing directly above the Carcere Mamertino on the Clivo Argentario. it.wikipedia places it "nel rione Campitelli" and says it was begun in 1597, completed in 1663 and consecrated on 11 November 1663.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the carpenters' confraternity had rented San Pietro in Carcere, inside the Mamertine below, from 1540.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Consolazione
places.summary: it.wikipedia places the church of Santa Maria della Consolazione in the rione Campitelli, on the square of the same name at the foot of the Tarpeian Rock, within the parish of Santa Maria in Portico in Campitelli and served by the Capuchins; it dates the earlier church's dedication to 3 November 1470 and the present building to 1585-1600. Overpass places the square itself in Ripa, and it.wikipedia's own rione article names piazza della Consolazione as the Ripa boundary.
places.history: it.wikipedia explains the dedication: the church was named "della consolazione" for the consoling of those condemned to death on the Tarpeian Rock above it, where sentences were carried out until 1550.

places.name: Chiesa di San Teodoro al Palatino
places.summary: A Greek Orthodox church on via di San Teodoro, under the north-west slope of the Palatine; it.wikipedia gives the religion as Orthodox Christian. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here. Note that via di San Teodoro is itself named by it.wikipedia's rione article as the boundary with Ripa.
places.history: it.wikipedia says the church was built in the sixth century on the ruins of the Horrea Agrippiana, probably reusing a pre-existing circular temple, with works continuing to 1705.

places.name: Basilica di Sant'Anastasia al Palatino
places.summary: A minor basilica on the Palatine slope above the Circus Maximus. it.wikipedia describes it as the national church for Rome's Peruvian community and for the Syro-Malabar Indian community, and as a stational church.
places.history: it.wikipedia says it was built in the first decades of the fourth century, giving 325-326 with a question mark, over earlier Roman structures beside the enclosure of the Circus Maximus, and that it is recorded as the titulus Anastasiae in the acts of the synod of 499.

places.name: Chiesa di San Sebastiano al Palatino
places.summary: A church on the Palatine, at the Vigna Barberini, run by the Fraternite Monastique de Jerusalem. The community's own site publishes the week: Sunday Eucharist 11.30, adoration 17.00-18.00 and Vespers 18.00; Tuesday to Thursday adoration from 17.00, Vespers 18.00 and Eucharist 18.30, with Thursday adoration continuing to 21.00; Saturday and Monday Eucharist 12.00, adoration from 17.00 and Vespers 18.00. Friday afternoon and Saturday morning are a community "desert" of silence.
places.history: it.wikipedia places the church "nel rione Campitelli", says a first building stood there in the tenth century and that the present arrangement dates from the rebuilding of 1624 under Urban VIII, and records the alternative name Santa Maria in Pallara.

places.name: Chiesa e convento di San Bonaventura al Palatino
places.summary: A church and convent on the south side of the Vigna Barberini, which it.wikipedia places "nel rione Campitelli". No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia says it was built in 1675 on the remains of a Roman cistern, for Cardinal Francesco Barberini at the request of Bonaventura da Barcellona, and names paintings by Giovanni Battista Benaschi and a Madonna del bell'amore of 1736-37 by Sebastiano Conca.

places.name: Chiesa di San Lorenzo in Miranda
places.summary: A church built inside the Tempio di Antonino e Faustina, in the Roman Forum.
places.history: it.wikipedia gives the church as seventh or eleventh century: the temple may have been reused as a church from the seventh century because it was believed to be the place where St Lawrence was condemned, but the church is attested in written sources only from the eleventh.

places.name: Nobile Collegio Chimico Farmaceutico
places.summary: The Roman pharmacists' college, in and above the church of San Lorenzo in Miranda inside the Temple of Antoninus and Faustina. It holds collections of pharmacy jars and mortars and a library with an online catalogue. Its site publishes no opening hours - only guided visits by booking - so plan ahead rather than turning up.
places.history: The college's own site records that on 8 March 1429 Pope Martin V gave the Corporazione dei Farmacisti Romani the collegiate church of San Lorenzo, erected inside the ancient Roman temple.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Annunziata a Tor de' Specchi
places.address: Via Tor de' Specchi, Roma RM
places.summary: it.wikipedia records that the church, in via Tor de' Specchi and attached to the monastery of Santa Francesca Romana, is open to the public only on 9 March, the saint's feast day; it corresponds to the medieval Santa Maria de Curte, was granted to the Oblates of Santa Francesca Romana after the monastery was founded in 1433, and was rebuilt in the early 18th century.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that two earlier fresco cycles of the saint's life survive in the oratory.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria Antiqua
places.summary: it.wikipedia describes Santa Maria Antiqua as a sixth-century church in the Forum, in the vestibule of Domitian's palace, together with the Oratory of the Forty Martyrs and the Domitianic ramp. No source states visiting arrangements for it, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the church of Santa Maria Liberatrice al Foro Romano was demolished in 1900 in order to excavate Santa Maria Antiqua beneath it.

places.name: Oratorio dei Quaranta Martiri
places.summary: A small oratory in the Forum, south of the Lacus Iuturnae. it.wikipedia says it was originally a quadrangular hall serving the ramp up to Domitian's palace, and that it was converted into a church with a small apse after the Byzantine capture of Rome under Narses in 552.

places.name: Foro Romano
places.summary: The Roman Forum is run by the Parco archeologico del Colosseo. The hours and price below are as the Sovrintendenza Capitolina publishes them, not as the Parco gives them. Opening is daily with last entry an hour before closing: 09.00-17.30 from 1 to 27 March, 09.00-19.15 from 28 March to 30 September, 09.00-18.30 from 1 to 24 October, 09.00-16.30 from 25 October to 28 February; 09.00-14.00 on 24 and 31 December; 08.30-16.30 on 1 January. The Forum Pass Super is given as EUR 18,00 full, valid for the day across the Foro Romano, the Fori Imperiali and the Palatino. Named tickets have been required for all admissions to the Parco archeologico del Colosseo since 18 October 2023. Check with the Parco before travelling.
places.history: The enclosure is one visit, not thirty. Besides the arches, temples and buildings with entries of their own in this guide, OpenStreetMap maps some three dozen further named features inside it, among them the Tempio di Vesta, the Tempio dei Dioscuri, the Tempio del Divo Giulio, the Tempio del Divo Romolo, the Tempio della Concordia, the Tempio di Vespasiano e Tito, the Portico degli Dei Consenti, the Basilica Aemilia with the Tabernae Novae, the Basilica Iulia, the Regia, the Domus Publica, the Rostra Vetera, the Umbilicus Urbis Romae, the Miliarium Aureum, the Lacus Iuturnae, the Horrea Agrippiana, the Vicus Tuscus, the Via Sacra, the Argiletum and the tomb of Giacomo Boni. A cafe, the Caffeteria del Parco, is mapped inside the enclosure, and OpenStreetMap also maps a ticket point for the Forum within the area.

places.name: Curia Iulia
places.summary: The Senate house, at the head of the Forum's short side between the Argiletum and the Comitium. it.wikipedia gives 29 BC to AD 526 as its span as the seat of the Senate, and records that the Curia Hostilia preceded it, was enlarged by Sulla in 80 BC as the Curia Cornelia, was damaged by fire in 52 BC, and was rebuilt monumentally in Caesar's works.
places.history: The building survives because it was a church from 630 until the 1930s. it.wikipedia records that Pope Honorius I built the church of Sant'Adriano al Foro Romano inside the Curia in 630, that Hadrian I raised it to a diaconia, that it was restored in 1228 under Gregory IX when the floor was raised three metres, and that it was deconsecrated and stripped back to the Curia in the 1930s. Curia and church are one building, not two sites.

places.name: Arco di Settimio Severo
places.summary: The triple triumphal arch at the north-west corner of the Forum, standing on a travertine plinth. it.wikipedia says it was erected in 202-203 and dedicated by the Senate to Septimius Severus and his sons Caracalla and Geta for the Parthian victories of 195 and 197-198, and gives its height as 23 m.
places.history: it.wikipedia notes that steps under the bays barred wheeled traffic through the arch.

places.name: Arco di Tito
places.summary: The single-bay arch on the east slope, at the Forum's eastern end. it.wikipedia dates it to the first century and reasons from the dedication: the Senate dedicated it to Titus as divus, so after his death and deification in 81, and it was complete by 90. It gives the height as 19.15 m.

places.name: Colonna di Foca
places.summary: An honorary column standing before the Rostra in the Forum. it.wikipedia records that it was dedicated, or rededicated, to the emperor Phocas on 1 August 608.

places.name: Tempio di Saturno
places.summary: A temple at the foot of the Capitoline, south-west of the imperial Rostra. it.wikipedia says it was built in the early Republic and restored repeatedly into the late fourth century.
places.history: The consecration date is not settled. it.wikipedia records two traditions: one giving Tullus Hostilius, the other the consulship of Aulus Sempronius Atratinus and Marcus Minucius Augurinus in 497 BC.

places.name: Tempio di Antonino e Faustina
places.summary: A temple north of the Regia, between the Basilica Aemilia and the Temple of Divus Romulus. it.wikipedia says it was erected after the empress's death in 141 and dedicated by the Senate, carrying the inscription DIVAE FAVSTINAE EX S C, and that on Antoninus's death in 161 the line DIVO ANTONINO ET was added above it.
places.history: The Nobile Collegio Chimico Farmaceutico's own site quotes the same inscription and the same 161 addition. The church of San Lorenzo in Miranda stands inside the temple.

places.name: Basilica di Massenzio
places.summary: A civil basilica on the Velia, at the Forum's eastern end. it.wikipedia says it was built by Maxentius between 308 and 312 and rededicated to Constantine, who replaced Maxentius's head on the colossal statue in the west apse, and gives its height as 35 m.
places.history: it.wikipedia records the building under the names Basilica Nova and Basilica Constantini.

places.name: Tempio di Venere e Roma
places.summary: A temple to Venus Felix and Roma Aeterna which it.wikipedia describes as occupying the whole space between the Basilica of Maxentius and the Colosseum. it.wikipedia names the emperor Hadrian himself as its architect and dates it begun in 121, inaugurated in 135 and finished in 141 under Antoninus Pius.
places.history: it.wikipedia says the site had previously held the atrium of Nero's Domus Aurea and the colossus, and repeats the classical anecdote that the colossus was moved with the help of twenty-four elephants.

places.name: Casa delle Vestali
places.summary: The Atrium Vestae, behind the Regia, which it.wikipedia describes as forming a unit with the Temple of Vesta. It says the residence itself joined the complex only from the second century BC.
places.history: it.wikipedia reports that recent excavation on the site found the remains of an eighth-century-BC hut.

places.name: Lapis Niger
places.summary: A patch of black paving over an archaic sacred area at the Comitium, which it.wikipedia says was sealed in the late Republic.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that it was rediscovered by Giacomo Boni on 10 January 1899.

places.name: Carcere Mamertino (Tullianum)
places.summary: Two superimposed levels of chambers cut into the south slope of the Capitoline beside the Scale Gemonie, below the church of San Giuseppe dei Falegnami. it.wikipedia dates the deeper level to the archaic period, the eighth to seventh century BC, and the upper to the Republic. No source states its hours or ticket prices, so none are given here.

places.name: Antiquarium Forense
places.address: Piazza Santa Maria Nova 53, Roma RM
places.summary: The Forum's own small museum, in rooms of the former monastery of Santa Francesca Romana. it.wikipedia says it was created in 1900 by Giacomo Boni, who excavated the Forum stratigraphically, to hold the finds and the records of his layers.
places.history: it.wikipedia, not the operator, gives the official name as Museo del Foro Romano.

places.name: Palatino
places.summary: The Palatine is one of Rome's seven hills, between the Velabrum and the Forum. it.wikipedia describes two summits, the higher called Palatium and the other Germalus or Cermalus. It is covered by the same Forum Pass Super the Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives as EUR 18,00 full, valid for the day across the Foro Romano, the Fori Imperiali and the Palatino.
places.history: As with the Forum, the hill is one visit rather than a list. Besides the buildings with entries of their own here, Overpass returns further named features on it with no per-place source: the Domus Severiana, the Terme Severiane, the Arcate severiane and the Terme di Massenzio on the southern extension, and the Capanne Romulee, the Auguratorium, the Tempio di Apollo, the Pedagogio, the Schola Praeconum, the Bagni di Livia, the Loggia Mattei, the Ninfeo degli Specchi, the Ninfeo della Pioggia, the cisterns, the central hypogean cryptoporticus and a chamber mapped only as "Ambiente 4". The Criptoportico Neroniano is mapped as an accessible footway. The sixteenth-century Horti Farnesiani, the Farnese gardens on the north side of the hill, have no article of their own on it.wikipedia - the name redirects to the article on the Palatine, which treats them as part of the hill rather than a separate site. No height is given: it.wikipedia's article body and its own infobox give different figures.

places.name: Domus Flavia
places.summary: The public wing of Domitian's palace, the western half of the complex on the Palatine. it.wikipedia says works began soon after the fire of 64, were directed by the architect Rabirio from 81, and concluded in 92.

places.name: Domus Augustana
places.summary: The private wing of the same palace, its eastern half. it.wikipedia gives it the same build and the same dates as the Domus Flavia: begun soon after the fire of 64, directed by Rabirio from 81, concluded in 92.

places.name: Stadio Palatino
places.summary: The third part of Domitian's palace, built after the other two. it.wikipedia describes it as brick, with Hadrianic work in the porticoes and Severan work in the exedra.

places.name: Settizonio
places.summary: The site of the Septizodium at the southern foot of the Palatine. it.wikipedia describes it as a monumental multi-storey nymphaeum facade raised by Septimius Severus in 203, forming the face of the Domus Severiana toward the Appian Way.
places.history: it.wikipedia gives its epoch as third to sixteenth century: it stood until it was demolished under Sixtus V.

places.name: Casa di Augusto
places.summary: Augustus's private house on the south-west slope of the Palatine. it.wikipedia repeats Suetonius: Augustus first lived above the scalae anulariae near the Velia, then moved to the Palatine into Hortensius's modest house. It is one of the ticketed Super sites within the archaeological area; no source states its price.

places.name: Casa di Livia
places.summary: A Republican house on the Palatine, excavated from 1869. it.wikipedia says the identification came from a lead pipe naming Iulia Aug(usta), found in Pietro Rosa's excavations for Napoleon III.
places.history: it.wikipedia notes that the earliest parts of the house date to 75-50 BC, and that it is now thought to have been an apartment for Livia within Augustus's house rather than a separate residence.

places.name: Casa dei Grifi
places.summary: A painted house of the Republican period on the Palatine, recorded by it.wikipedia.

places.name: Elagabalium (Vigna Barberini)
places.summary: it.wikipedia describes the Elagabalium as the temple to Sol Invictus, later to Jupiter, at the north-east corner of the Palatine, on the terrace known as the Vigna Barberini. The churches of San Sebastiano al Palatino and San Bonaventura al Palatino stand on the same terrace.

places.name: Museo Palatino (Antiquarium del Palatino)
places.summary: The museum of the Palatine, on the hill itself. it.wikipedia records that an earlier Antiquarium was created in the later nineteenth century by Pietro Rosa in a Farnese building.
places.history: it.wikipedia says that building was demolished by Rodolfo Lanciani in 1882 to link the Forum and Palatine excavations, and the collections went to the Terme di Diocleziano; the present museum stems from Alfonso Bartoli's initiative in the 1930s.

places.name: Foro di Cesare
places.summary: One of the five Imperial Fora, on the Campitelli side of via dei Fori Imperiali. it.wikipedia says Caesar inaugurated it while it was still incomplete on 26 September 46 BC, the last day of his four triumphs, and that it was completed under Augustus.
places.history: The Sovrintendenza Capitolina's walkway through the Imperial Fora leaves at the Foro di Cesare on via Bonella, having passed beneath via dei Fori Imperiali from the Trajan's Column end in Monti. The Basilica Argentaria and the Tempio di Venere Genitrice are mapped in the same block.

places.name: Foro di Nerva (Foro Transitorio)
places.summary: An imperial forum on the Campitelli side of via dei Fori Imperiali, also called the Foro Transitorio. it.wikipedia says it was built by Domitian and already conceived in 85-86 according to Martial, and that it was inaugurated together with the temple of Minerva in late 97 by Nerva, after Domitian's murder.
places.history: The temple of Minerva and the Porticus absidata belong to this forum rather than standing on their own: the Comune's own page on the Foro di Nerva places the Porticus absidata "alle spalle del tempio di Minerva", behind the temple, inside the forum.

places.name: Tempio della Pace
places.summary: Also called the Foro della Pace, on the south side of via dei Fori Imperiali and so on the Campitelli side of the boundary, as it.wikipedia's article describes it.
places.history: The basilica of Santi Cosma e Damiano is built into the Temple of Peace, which is the clearest physical link between the rione's churches and its archaeology.

places.name: Via Alessandrina
places.summary: A street that mostly no longer exists. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina records that Cardinal Michele Bonelli (1541-1598), a nephew of Pius V, laid out this area in the later sixteenth century, and that the street - named Alessandrina after the cardinal - was opened in 1584 and was more than 400 metres long. It was largely destroyed in the 1930s.

places.name: Piazza d'Aracoeli
places.summary: The square at the foot of the Capitoline, running from via del Teatro di Marcello to via di Tor Margana; it.wikipedia's infobox gives its rione as Campitelli. it.wikipedia says it was formerly the piazza del Mercato, divided into Mercato and Mercatello.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the square lost a whole side, first to the Vittoriano works from 1885 and then to the isolamento of the Capitoline in the 1930s. Palazzo Fani stands at its corner with via della Tribuna di Tor de' Specchi and Palazzo Massimo di Rignano at its corner with via del Teatro di Marcello.

places.name: Fontana di piazza d'Aracoeli
places.summary: The fountain in piazza d'Aracoeli. The Sovrintendenza Capitolina gives the author as Giacomo della Porta (1533-1602), dates it 1589, describes it in marble and travertine originally fed by the Acqua Felice, and names the sculptors Andrea Brasca, Pietro Gucci and Pace Naldini.
places.history: The same page records that the wide circular basin at the base was added around 1860, and that the fountain was restored in 2025 under the PNRR Caput Mundi programme.

places.name: Palazzo Maccarini Odescalchi
places.summary: Palazzo Maccarini Odescalchi, on piazza Margana; it.wikipedia's Campitelli article describes it as a 17th-century Mannerist building.

places.name: Palazzo Muti Bussi
places.summary: it.wikipedia gives the address as "via dell'Aracoeli, 2 (Rione X Campitelli)" and says Giacomo Della Porta designed and began the palace about 1585 for Orazio Muti; after Della Porta's death Giovanni Antonio De Rossi worked on it in 1642-45 and completed the entrances and the courtyard in 1660-62.
places.history: it.wikipedia says the palace was modernised in the eighteenth century and took its present name when Cecilia Muti married Count Giulio Bussi in the early nineteenth. The article also gives the building five facades, which is why it.wikipedia's rione article lists it on via di San Venanzio while the palace's own article gives via dell'Aracoeli. The two are not in conflict.

places.name: Palazzo Fani
places.summary: Palazzo Fani, at the corner of piazza d'Aracoeli and via della Tribuna di Tor de' Specchi. it.wikipedia describes it as Mannerist and credits Giacomo Della Porta with its renewal for the Fani; its rione article adds a raising by Giovanni Battista Giovenale in 1885-88. The two Wikipedia pages give different dates and neither is a primary source.
places.history: it.wikipedia also records that the palace was let to Cardinal Federico Borromeo in 1599.

places.name: Palazzo Massimo di Rignano
places.summary: A palace on piazza d'Aracoeli at the corner with via del Teatro di Marcello. it.wikipedia places it in the rione Campitelli, calls it Baroque with a structure of fifteenth-century origin built for the Boccabella, and credits Carlo Fontana with its remodelling for the Massimo di Rignano.
places.history: it.wikipedia's rione article gives a different account of the same building: seventeenth century, dated 1696, also crediting Carlo Fontana. The two pages disagree and neither is a primary source, so both readings are given here rather than one being chosen.

places.name: Palazzo Albertoni Spinola
places.summary: A palace at piazza Campitelli 2, which it.wikipedia says "si trova nel Rione X (Campitelli)". it.wikipedia credits Giacomo Della Porta and Girolamo Rainaldi, dates the work to about 1580 to about 1616, and names Baldassarre Paluzzi Albertoni as the man who commissioned it.
places.history: The square in front of it is a different question from the building. it.wikipedia's rione article names piazza di Campitelli as the boundary with Sant'Angelo while also listing it among Campitelli's squares, so this guide makes no claim about the square itself - only about the palace, whose own article states its rione in terms.

places.name: Teatro della Cometa
places.summary: Teatro della Cometa, a working theatre in the rione, at teatrodellacometa.com.

places.name: Antica Trattoria Angelino
places.summary: A restaurant at Piazza Margana 37. "Antica" in a business name is not evidence of how long it has traded.

places.name: Eduardo II
places.summary: A restaurant at Vicolo Margana 14. No source states more than the name and the address.

places.name: DIDDIBISTRO
places.summary: A restaurant at Piazza d'Aracoeli 4. No source states more than the name and the address.

places.name: Antico Caffe del Teatro Marcello
places.address: Via del Teatro di Marcello 42, Roma RM
places.summary: A cafe at Via del Teatro di Marcello 42. Name and address only: as with the trattoria on piazza Margana, "Antico" in the name is not evidence of age. The street is in Campitelli even though the Theatre of Marcellus it is named for is not.

places.name: Bar Campidoglio
places.summary: A cafe at Piazza d'Aracoeli 11. No source states more than the name and the address.

places.name: Caffe Rudy
places.summary: A cafe at Piazza d'Aracoeli 15. No source states more than the name and the address.

entries.name: Cordonata Capitolina
entries.note: The ramped stair up from via del Teatro di Marcello, designed 1534-38 by Michelangelo for Paul III and partly modified by Giacomo Della Porta, with the Dioscuri set on the balustrade in 1583 and the Trofei di Mario in 1590.

entries.name: Piazza del Campidoglio
entries.note: The paving, palaces and sculpture were carried out over centuries to a design of about the middle of the sixteenth century; the square sits in the valley between the hill's two ancient summits, whose level was some eight metres lower.

entries.name: Musei Capitolini
entries.note: The museum dates its birth to 1471, when Sixtus IV gave a group of bronze statues to the Roman people; the Lupa Capitolina is held here, and opening is daily 09.30-19.30 with last admission an hour before closing.

entries.name: Basilica di Santa Maria in Aracoeli
entries.note: Reached by the Scalinata dell'Ara Coeli on the Arx, the hill's northern summit; Gothic then Baroque, built from the thirteenth century to the eighteenth, and called Santa Maria in Capitolio before the present name appears in 1323.

entries.name: Vittoriano (Monumento Nazionale a Vittorio Emanuele II)
entries.note: Giuseppe Sacconi built it from 1885 to 1905 and it opened on 4 June 1911, the fiftieth anniversary of unification; the burial of the Unknown Soldier turned it into a shrine, and its basements sheltered Roman civilians late in the Second World War.

entries.name: Terrazza Panoramica del Vittoriano
entries.note: Lifts reach the roof at seventy metres for a 360-degree view, with two bronze quadrigas at the lift exit standing for the Unity and the Liberty of Italy.

entries.name: Foro Romano
entries.note: One ticketed enclosure rather than thirty separate sites, run by the Parco archeologico del Colosseo; the EUR 18,00 Forum Pass Super covers it with the Fori Imperiali and the Palatino for the day, and named tickets have been required since 18 October 2023.

entries.name: Curia Iulia
entries.note: Seat of the Senate from 29 BC to AD 526, and standing today because Honorius I built the church of Sant'Adriano inside it in 630; it was stripped back to the Curia in the 1930s.

entries.name: Arco di Settimio Severo
entries.note: Erected in 202-203 at the Forum's north-west corner and dedicated by the Senate for the Parthian victories of 195 and 197-198; 23 m high, with steps under the bays that barred wheeled traffic.

entries.name: Arco di Tito
entries.note: A single bay 19.15 m high at the Forum's eastern end, dedicated to Titus as divus and so raised after his death in 81, complete by 90.

entries.name: Basilica di Massenzio
entries.note: Built on the Velia between 308 and 312 and rededicated to Constantine, who replaced Maxentius's head on the colossal statue in the west apse; the vaults stand 35 m.

entries.name: Palatino
entries.note: The hill between the Velabrum and the Forum, with two summits, Palatium and Germalus, and the sixteenth-century Farnese gardens on its north side; the same Forum Pass Super admits you.

entries.name: Foro di Cesare
entries.note: Caesar inaugurated it still incomplete on 26 September 46 BC, the last day of his four triumphs, and it was finished under Augustus; the Imperial Fora walkway comes out here on via Bonella.

entries.name: Carcere Mamertino (Tullianum)
entries.note: Two superimposed chambers cut into the Capitoline's south slope beside the Scale Gemonie, the deeper dated to the eighth to seventh century BC and the upper to the Republic.

links.note: Via dei Fori Imperiali is the boundary. Trajan's Forum, Column and Markets are Monti's; the Imperial Fora walkway starts there and ends in Campitelli.
